newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan laid tightening ground - ex-Fed Blinder.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan laid tightening ground - ex-Fed Blinder.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan has laid the ground for an upcoming tightening of U.S. credit, former Fed Vice Chairman Alan Blinder said on Friday.

"There is very little doubt that the Chairman has been for a few months now laying down the predicate for a rate increase if he chooses to do so," Blinder said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television.
Blinder, however, declined to predict the outcome of the Match 25 Federal Open Market Committee's meeting, which he described as "an extremely close call."

Blinder said that if he still were at the Fed he would not vote for a tightening because the "experiment" the Fed has been running to let growth rise and unemployment slip has so far not resulted in higher inflation.

"This experiment is running extremely well right now. If I were still a voting member of the FOMC, I would be inclined to let run a little longer until I saw some real signs it was not working," said Blinder, who now holds the chair of economics at Princeton University.
Blinder left the Fed Board in early 1996. He never dissented throughout the 1994-1995 tightening cycle.
"The risks are fairly finely balanced," Blinder said. "But the risks are clear, if you stand pat longer than you should, you risk an acceleration of inflation."
Blinder said another risk for the Fed is to tighten credit when not needed, which would weigh on growth and jobs.
Answering a question about the level of the non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment (NAIRU), Blinder said "prevailing wisdom is more around 5.5 percent."
"Maybe two years from now... the NAIRU may be as low as 5.25 percent," the Princeton University professor said.
